title: The lesson after the absence matters
author: Shaun Allison
summary: Shaun Allison argues that attendance work is not only about letters, phone calls and percentages but also about what happens in the first lesson after a pupil returns from absence. He notes that national absence in autumn and spring 2025/26 was 6.6% against rates consistently below 5% before the pandemic, and describes a cycle in which absence creates gaps, gaps make lessons harder, pupils feel less successful and connected, and returning becomes harder still. The best teachers, he says, avoid making absence a pupil's public identity, welcoming them back warmly without sarcasm or interrogation. They also avoid trying to reteach every missed lesson or lowering expectations; instead they identify the essential knowledge or vocabulary missed and give the smallest support needed to reconnect the pupil. He ties this to responsive teaching in his school's Inclusion Strategy and concludes that every lesson contributes to a pupil's daily judgement about whether school is a place where they belong and can succeed.
points: Absence sets off a vicious cycle of knowledge gaps, lower success and belonging, and further absence, so the return lesson is a pivotal moment.
Welcome pupils back warmly and privately; sarcastic remarks or public questioning make absence part of their identity.
Do not reteach everything and do not lower expectations: prioritise the essential knowledge and vocabulary needed to access current learning.
Attendance improvement depends on classroom experience as well as sanctions and contact, because pupils judge daily whether school feels like somewhere they can succeed.
quotes: Attendance has become one of the most stubborn challenges facing secondary schools since the pandemic. Like most schools, it’s something we are working on at Durrington.
Absence creates gaps in learning → gaps make lessons harder → students feel less successful and less connected → returning becomes harder → further absence becomes more likely.
Imagine being a student returning after several days, or perhaps several weeks, away. You walk into a classroom where everybody else seems to know what is happening. Books have moved on.

The best teachers therefore avoid making absence the student’s public identity. There is no sarcastic “Nice of you to join us” or public interrogation about where they have been. Instead, the student is calmly and warmly welcomed back into the normal life of the classroom.

Crucially, this does not mean attempting to reteach every missed lesson. Nor should it mean lowering expectations. It means identifying the essential knowledge or vocabulary the student has missed and providing the smallest amount of additional support needed to reconnect them with current learning.

Effective teachers prioritise instead. They distinguish between what would be nice to catch up and the essential knowledge the student needs in order to access future learning. That distinction matters.

This is exactly the kind of responsive, adaptive teaching described in our Inclusion Strategy: high-quality universal classroom teaching combined with precise additional support, without reducing ambition.

That is why attendance improvement is not solely about letters, phone calls, sanctions or percentages. Those things have their place, but students also make daily judgements about whether school feels like somewhere in which they belong and can succeed. Every lesson contributes to that judgement.
